headline: Breakthrough: Scientists Crack the Code on Recycling Acrylic Glass
meta_description: Researchers at ETH Zurich have developed a simple, low-energy method to recycle acrylic glass into virgin-quality material, recovering up to 98% of the origina…
summary_short: ETH Zurich researchers have solved a decades-old recycling puzzle: turning acrylic glass waste back into pure, reusable material using minimal heat and existing equipmen…
body:
Researchers at ETH Zurich have cracked a problem that has frustrated the recycling industry for decades. They've developed a practical method to break down acrylic glass—the material behind Plexiglas brand windows, car taillights, and protective barriers—back into its original building blocks with remarkable purity. Using a single inexpensive chemical already available commercially, the team recovered up to 98% of the material as pure monomers, even when the original acrylic contained dyes or impurities. What makes this genuinely transformative is the efficiency: the process requires temperatures just over 200°C—roughly half what previous methods demanded—and needs no solvents at all.

For decades, acrylic glass has piled up in landfills because existing recycling approaches were too costly, too energy-intensive, or too technically complex for companies to justify. The new method changes the economics entirely. Because it works with equipment manufacturers already have and integrates into standard processes, businesses wouldn't need expensive facility overhauls to adopt it. The recovered material reaches a quality high enough to manufacture new products indistinguishable from virgin plastic.

ETH Zurich has already filed a patent and is actively seeking industry partners to scale the innovation. The team's work, published in Nature Chemistry, hints at something larger: the same basic approach may eventually work for other common plastics like polystyrene. For a material embedded in millions of everyday products worldwide, this represents a genuine turning point—the kind of practical innovation that could meaningfully reduce plastic waste while actually making financial sense for manufacturers.
quick_facts: ETH Zurich researchers developed a new acrylic glass recycling method
Process recovers up to 98% of material as pure monomers
Requires just over 200°C — half the heat of previous methods
Works with existing factory equipment, no expensive overhauls needed
Recovered material is pure enough to make new virgin-quality products
